Every Friday Ira came home to the Kolkata flat for dinner, and every Friday the table got a little quieter. At nineteen she had joined a group that met in a rented hall near Gariahat, and lately she spoke of 'the outside world' as if her family lived in it.
Her mother, Aadhya, had wanted to shout more than once. Instead she kept cooking the shukto Ira loved and kept asking questions.
Tonight, over the fish, she asked, 'What do they give you there that you didn't get here?'
Ira looked up, wary, waiting for a joke. None came. 'They listen to me,' she said at last. 'Nobody interrupts.'
Aadhya nodded slowly. 'I interrupt too much. I'm sorry.' She passed the rice. 'Tell me about one person there you like.'
Ira talked for twenty minutes. When she left, Aadhya hugged her at the door and said, 'Come next Friday. Always.'

qa.q: What did Aadhya keep cooking for Ira?
qa.a: She kept cooking the shukto Ira loved.

qa.q: Why was Ira wary when her mother asked the question?
qa.a: She expected to be mocked or lectured about the group, so she waited for a joke before answering.

qa.q: Why is Aadhya's way of talking to Ira wise at this stage?
qa.a: She keeps affection, avoids ridicule and asks open questions, which keeps Ira talking and keeps the way home open.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel as she hugs Ira at the door?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel relieved and hopeful after hearing Ira talk for twenty minutes, and wants Ira to know home is always open.

grounding: It shows a mother keeping affection, avoiding ridicule and asking what the group gives her daughter, preserving the path back.

'Aadhya, sit. I made coffee.'
'If this is another talk about the group, Ira-akka, I'm leaving.'
'It isn't a talk. It's coffee.' Ira pushed the steel tumbler across the table in their Chennai kitchen. 'Too much sugar, like you like it.'
Aadhya sat, arms folded.
'Can I ask something? Not to argue.'
'You'll say they're brainwashing me. Appa already said it.'
'I won't. I'm asking what it's given you. Honestly.'
A long pause. 'Friends. People who call me back. A reason to get up.'
'That's a lot,' Ira said. 'I didn't know you were missing that.'
Aadhya's arms loosened. 'You're not going to laugh at them?'
'No. I just want to know you. Whatever you're doing.'
'They say families try to pull you out.'
'I'm not pulling. I'm here. Same kitchen. Same terrible coffee.' Aadhya almost smiled.
'Come on Sunday?' Ira asked.
'Maybe.'

When my younger sister Vidya came home at Diwali, she called our parents "asleep" within an hour. Everything was "the Path" this and "outsiders" that. My first instinct was to laugh and say something sharp. I'd done that at Holi, and she hadn't spoken to me for two months.
So this time I bit my tongue. I made her the ginger tea she likes and asked, "What does the group give you that you weren't getting here?"
She looked surprised. Then she talked for an hour: about feeling invisible at college, about people there who listen, about purpose. Some of it hurt to hear. Some of it was fair.
I didn't argue. I just asked more questions, and told her I love her and our door is always open, whatever she decides.
She hugged me before she left. It was brief. But it was a hug. I'm Eshaan, and I'm keeping that door open.

qa.q: What tea did Eshaan make for Vidya?
qa.a: The ginger tea she likes.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when the urge to laugh came?
qa.a: Eshaan felt irritated and hurt by her words, but held back, remembering how ridicule at Holi had cost two months of silence.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan's open question work better than an argument?
qa.a: It showed care and curiosity, letting Vidya explain what the group gives her, which keeps trust and the way home open.

qa.q: What might Vidya have felt when asked what the group gives her?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and relieved to be asked rather than mocked, which let her speak honestly.

grounding: A sibling keeps affection, avoids ridicule and asks what the group has given a young sister, keeping the way back open.

Family counsellor's note, session 4
Suraj came alone again. His daughter Kalyani is still living with the group and calls home rarely. Two months ago he told me he had shouted that she'd joined "a bunch of fools"; she hung up and didn't call for three weeks.
Since then he has changed his approach. He sends her a short, warm message every Sunday: a photo of the jasmine she planted, news of the dog. No arguments, no jokes about the group. When she called last week and said outsiders are blind, he didn't argue. He asked, "What has the group given you that you needed?" She talked about feeling useful.
He told me it was the longest call they have had in a year. He cried in my office, then laughed at himself.
Plan: continue weekly contact, keep asking open questions, and prepare him for a slow process.

qa.q: What does Suraj send Kalyani every Sunday?
qa.a: A short, warm message: a photo of the jasmine she planted, news of the dog.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel after the longest call in a year?
qa.a: He felt relieved and moved, crying and then laughing at himself in the office.

qa.q: Why is Suraj's new approach more likely to work than shouting?
qa.a: Warm weekly contact without ridicule, and open questions, keep Kalyani connected and preserve the path back the group tries to close.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt when her father asked what the group gave her?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and respected, which let her talk about feeling useful instead of defending herself.

grounding: A counsellor notes a father who stops ridiculing, keeps warm contact and asks his daughter open questions about what the group gives her.

Guwahati, Thursday night
Mousumi came home for two days. She said our parents "live in darkness" and that her group's leader is "the only one telling the truth". Deuta's face went red. I could feel a shouting match coming.
Then I remembered what Yusuf at work told me, from his own years in a group like that: "Whatever you do, don't laugh at them. Laughing just proves the group right about outsiders."
So after dinner I took her out for momos, just us, like old times. I asked, "What do you love most about them?" She said they made her feel important. I asked what she missed about home. She went quiet, then said, "Your terrible singing."
I didn't win any argument today. I didn't try. But she laughed twice, and she let me walk her to the bus. Door still open.
Bhupen

qa.q: Where did Bhupen take Mousumi after dinner?
qa.a: Out for momos, just us, like old times.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when a shouting match seemed close?
qa.a: Bhupen felt tense and worried, then chose calm, remembering Yusuf's warning not to laugh at her.

qa.q: Which question helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what she missed about home, because it gently reminded Mousumi of the bond without attacking the group.

qa.q: What was the evening like for Mousumi?
qa.a: She likely felt cared for rather than judged, laughing twice and letting Bhupen walk her to the bus.

grounding: A family member avoids ridicule, keeps affection and asks open questions about what the group gives, preserving the path home.
